intro.html: Writers describe the old and the new with surprising precision. A thing can be ancient and admired, or old and laughed at, or simply out of date; something new can be fresh, clever or startlingly experimental.

Very old: primeval (from the first ages), archaic (no longer used), hoary (gray with age), antiquated and antediluvian (out of date, often a joke). Unspoiled: pristine. Missing the old days: nostalgia. New: novel, innovative, avant-garde.
Two Latin roots do most of the work: nov means new (novel, innovative, renovate), and antiqu and ante point back to old and before.

words.def: very old, or no longer in everyday use
words.ctx: The town still settled its disputes with a set of {archaic} rules written in 1790, long after every other town had updated theirs.
words.etym: From Greek archaikos, “old-fashioned,” from archaios (ancient), from arche (beginning).

mn.cue: ARCH-aic: as old as a crumbling ARCH
mn.text: Among the broken columns, Professor Edwin reads aloud from a crumbling scroll: “Hark! Thou art welcome!” Words that old, no longer used, are {archaic}.

scene.alt: Among ancient ruins, an old professor reads old-fashioned words from a scroll while a boy looks puzzled.

words.ex: The office still used an {antiquated} fax machine that jammed every afternoon.
words.ctx: Compared with the bright new library across town, the old building, with its {antiquated} card catalog and flickering lamps, felt like a museum.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin antiquus (old, ancient), the source of antique.

mn.cue: ANTIQUE-ATED: belongs in an ANTIQUE shop
mn.text: Uncle Marcus still listens to the news on a radio the size of a suitcase that crackles more than it talks; it belongs in an antique shop. It is {antiquated}.

scene.alt: A man listens happily to a huge old radio while a teen holding a phone laughs.

words.def: extremely old or old-fashioned (often said as a joke)
words.ex: My uncle’s {antediluvian} computer takes ten minutes to start.
words.ctx: The students giggled at the teacher’s {antediluvian} slides, full of cartoons and fonts that had gone out of style before any of them were born.
words.etym: From Latin ante (before) + diluvium (flood): literally, from before the great flood of ancient stories.

mn.text: Uncle Victor rides to town in a creaky wooden cart pulled by an old horse, while the kids zoom past on skateboards; his ride seems to date from before the great flood. It is {antediluvian}.

scene.alt: A man rides a creaky wooden cart pulled by a sleepy horse while a teen on a skateboard laughs.

words.def: very old; gray or white with age
words.ex: The {hoary} old oak had stood in the village square for three hundred years.
words.ctx: The comedian’s act was full of {hoary} jokes that audiences had been groaning at since their grandparents’ day.
words.etym: From hoar, an old word for gray or white, as in hoarfrost.
words.note: Hoary can describe gray hair or an idea worn out by long use: a hoary old joke.

mn.text: Professor Edwin’s beard is so long and white that it looks dusted with frost; he is {hoary} with age.

scene.alt: An old professor with a long white beard waves in the falling snow.

words.def: belonging to the earliest ages of the world
words.ex: The explorers hiked through a {primeval} forest of giant ferns and moss-covered trees.
words.ctx: The cave paintings date from a {primeval} time, thousands of years before anyone had built a city or written a single word.
words.etym: From Latin primaevus, “in the first age”: primus (first) + aevum (age).

mn.text: Deep in the jungle, Sami finds a valley where giant plants tower overhead and a dragon-sized lizard dozes, as if the world’s first age had never ended; the place is {primeval}.

scene.alt: An explorer points at a giant sleeping lizard in a jungle that looks untouched since the first ages.

words.ex: The old comic book was in {pristine} condition, without a single crease.
words.ctx: Before the resort was built, the beach was {pristine}: no footprints, no litter, just smooth sand and clear water.
words.note: Pristine means unspoiled, as it was at first, not merely clean.

mn.cue: PRIS-TINE: fresh snow no one has touched
mn.text: Ivy steps outside at dawn and finds the field covered in smooth new snow, without a single footprint; she can hardly bear to walk on it, because it is {pristine}.

scene.alt: A girl tiptoes at the edge of a sparkling field of fresh, untouched snow.

words.def: a fond, wistful longing for the past
words.ex: The smell of popcorn filled Grandpa with {nostalgia} for the movie theater of his childhood.
words.ctx: Paging through the old photo album, Mom felt a wave of {nostalgia}: the treehouse, the bicycle with streamers, the summer evenings that seemed to last forever.
words.etym: From Greek nostos (a return home) + algos (pain): it first named homesickness.

mn.cue: NOST-ALGIA: a sweet ACHE for the past
mn.text: Granny Mae turns the pages of her old photo album and smiles at her first bicycle and her childhood dog; the sweet ache she feels is {nostalgia}.

labels.text: NOST-ALGIA: a sweet ACHE for the PAST

scene.alt: A grandmother smiles fondly over an old photo album, remembering her childhood.

words.ex: Using a kite to deliver the birthday card was a {novel} idea.
words.ctx: The inventor’s solution was {novel}: instead of building a bigger dam, she planted thousands of trees upstream to slow the floodwater.
words.note: As a noun, a novel is a long story. As an adjective, novel means new and different.

mn.text: Sami builds a little robot that walks the dog for him, leash and all; no one in town has seen anything like it. The idea is {novel}.

scene.alt: A proud boy watches the little robot he built walk his dog through the park.

words.def: bringing in new ideas or ways of doing things
words.ex: The school’s {innovative} garden program teaches math through planting.
words.ctx: Rather than copy the other bakeries, Nell was {innovative}, inventing flavors no one had ever tried, like lemon-basil scones and pepper-honey cookies.
words.etym: From Latin innovare, “to renew, to make new”: in- (into) + novare (to make new), from novus (new).

mn.text: Nell bakes cookies no one has ever tasted, pepper-honey and lemon-basil, and hangs a sign saying NEW FLAVORS; she is {innovative}.

scene.alt: A baker with a bright idea offers a new kind of cookie under a sign announcing new flavors.

words.def: new and experimental, especially in the arts
words.ex: The museum’s new wing shows {avant-garde} paintings that look nothing like traditional art.
words.ctx: In its day the composer’s music was {avant-garde}, full of clashing sounds that shocked audiences; today the same pieces are played at school concerts.
words.etym: From French avant (before, ahead) + garde (guard): the vanguard, the front part of an army that marches ahead of the rest.

mn.text: Nell paints with her feet, her elbows and a dripping mop, far ahead of what anyone else is trying; her art is {avant-garde}.

scene.alt: An artist in a beret dances wildly before her experimental painting while an old man scratches his head.

after.html: Pristine does not just mean clean: a pristine forest is untouched by people, and a pristine old book is still as it was when new. A hoary joke is not white-haired; it is just very old.

items.q: Which sentence uses pristine in its careful sense?
choices: The lake was pristine: no one had ever built on its shores.
I wiped the kitchen counter until it was pristine for a minute.
The pristine kitten was very hungry.
items.why: Pristine means unspoiled, in its original state. The lake untouched by building is pristine.

items.q: “The scientist proposed a novel solution.” Here novel means…
items.why: As an adjective, novel means new and different. As a noun, a novel is a book-length story.
ante (before) + diluvium (flood): from before the great flood of ancient stories, and so extremely old-fashioned.
nostos (return home) + algos (pain): nostalgia first named homesickness, a painful longing for home.
